outline.description: This chapter establishes the factual matrix of the crime, detailing the domestic incident involving Justin Cutbank, the subsequent standoff with law enforcement, and the recovery of physical evidence. It outlines the charges brought against Cutbank under 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(1) and 924(e), summarizes the jury's findings regarding his status as a felon and his prior violent felony convictions, and defines the appellate scope, focusing on challenges to evidentiary rulings and the application of a specific sentencing enhancement.
subtopics: The November 2020 Domestic Incident: Assault, Kidnapping, and Flight
Police Standoff and Recovery of Physical Evidence (DNA match, sawed-off rifle)
Charges: Felon in Possession and Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA) Applicability
Procedural History: Conviction, Sentencing Range Calculation, and Grounds for Appeal

outline.chapter_title: Admissibility of Prior Acts as Intrinsic Evidence
outline.description: This section analyzes the First Circuit's rejection of Cutbank's argument that testimony regarding his prior observation of the specific firearm violated Federal Rule of Evidence 404(b). It explains the distinction between 'other acts' evidence (propensity) and 'intrinsic' evidence directly relevant to establishing possession and continuity. The chapter details why witnesses testifying to having seen Cutbank with the sawed-off rifle before the incident was admissible to prove ownership and control rather than character.
subtopics: Rule 404(b) Analysis: Propensity vs. Intrinsic Evidence Distinction
Relevance Test: Establishing Continuous Possession via Prior Sightings
Application to Witness Testimony from D.F. and C.F.
Standard of Review for Pre-Trial Evidentiary Rulings

outline.chapter_title: Confrontation Clause Rights and Hearsay Limitations
outline.description: Covering procedural due process concerns, this chapter examines Cutbank's claims regarding hearsay statements made by victims to police before trial. It clarifies the requirements for limiting instructions on hearsay used solely for context versus substantive proof. Furthermore, it addresses Confrontation Clause violations by explaining how the victims' live testimony at trial cured potential constitutional defects regarding out-of-court statements.
subtopics: Hearsay Rules: Contextual Use vs. Substantive Evidence
'Abuse of Discretion' Standard for Denying Limiting Instructions
Satisfaction of Confrontation Clause Requirements through Live Testimony
(Unpreserved Error): Authentication Standards for Extrinsic Impeachment Evidence

outline.description: This chapter focuses on the core sentencing dispute: whether a four-level enhancement applied when Cutbank possessed a firearm in connection with another felony offense (domestic violence/kidnapping). It breaks down the text of USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B), explains that a separate conviction is not required for this enhancement, and discusses why the district court properly adopted factual findings from the Presentence Investigation Report (PSR). It also addresses the interaction between this enhancement and ACCA guideline calculations.
subtopics: (Interpretation): Meaning of 'In Connection With' Another Felony Offense
(Requirement): Necessity of a Separate Conviction or Charge
(Fact-Finding): Reliance on PSR Facts Without Objection at Sentencing
(Guideline Interaction): Calculating Offense Levels under ACCA vs. § 2K2.1 Enhancements

outline.description: (The final chapter evaluates Cutbank's argument that his sentence was substantively unreasonable despite falling within the advisory guidelines range.) It reviews (the standard presumption of reasonableness for within-guidelines sentences,) analyzing whether (the district court adequately considered § 3553(a) factors.) The chapter concludes by examining why (the severity of Cutbank's conduct—including domestic abuse, kidnapping, and assaulting an officer—supported a lengthy prison term without requiring a variance.)
subtopics: (Analysis): Harmless Error Standard Applied to Cumulative Trial Errors
(Conclusion): Overwhelming Government Evidence Renders Any Error Non-Reversible

outline.chapter_title: Final Synthesis: Affirmance Based on Record Strength
outline.description: The concluding chapter synthesizes how both legal prongs—the lack of prejudicial error at trial and the procedural/substantive validity of the sentence—lead to affirmation. It emphasizes that even if minor evidentiary errors occurred (which they did not), they were harmless given the strength of DNA evidence, victim identification, and statutory enhancements.
subtopics: Cumulative Effect Doctrine in Eighth Circuit Jurisprudence
Presumption of Reasonableness for Within-Guidelines Sentences
Summary Judgment Logic in Appellate Review
